_about: Career goals (milestones). The engine scores and schedules these. Term codes: 1F = year 1 fall, 1S = spring, 1U = summer after year 1, … 4S, then G1/G2 = first two terms after graduation. window = earliest term it makes sense, the ideal range, and the latest useful term. steps: 3–6 concrete actions in order. doneWhen: how the student knows it's finished. guides: how-to pages (resources of type guide, or other non-Rutgers resources) shown with the steps; the engine never reads steps, doneWhen, or guides. forNextYear: a yearly goal that pays off the following school year (FAFSA, outside scholarships), so there is no round in the final year. late: title, steps, and doneWhen to use when the goal is scheduled after its ideal window, so early-college goals read right for upper-year students.

goals.title: Meet a career advisor and sketch a 4-year plan
goals.why: Gets a human in your corner early and surfaces campus programs you'd miss.
steps: Book a 30-minute appointment with your campus career center through Handshake.
Bring your current resume (a rough draft is fine) and two or three fields you're curious about.
Ask which campus programs, clubs, and deadlines matter for those fields this year.
Leave with a written semester-by-semester plan and the date of your next check-in.
goals.doneWhen: You have a written 4-year plan you made with an advisor and a follow-up date on your calendar.

late.title: Meet a career advisor and plan your remaining semesters
steps: Book a 30-minute appointment with your campus career center through Handshake.
Bring your resume and the roles or programs you are aiming for after graduation.
Ask what to prioritize in the semesters you have left: applications, deadlines, and campus programs.
Leave with a short plan through graduation and the date of your next check-in.
late.doneWhen: You have a plan for your remaining semesters, made with an advisor, and a follow-up date on your calendar.
late.why: An advisor can point you to what matters most in the time you have left, and to campus programs you might miss.

goals.title: Complete your Handshake profile
goals.why: Your campus's employers and career fairs run through Handshake.
steps: Sign in to your campus Handshake with your NetID and upload your resume so it fills in your education and experience.
Add a clear photo, your major and graduation date, at least 5 skills, and your clubs or jobs.
List your job interests (roles, industries, and locations) so Handshake recommends the right postings.
Make your profile visible to employers in your privacy settings.
Follow 10 employers you'd like to work for so their events and postings reach you.
goals.doneWhen: Handshake shows your profile as complete, employers can see it, and you follow at least 10 employers.

goals.title: Write your first college resume
goals.why: Nearly every application below needs one.
steps: Read a first-year resume guide and look at two or three sample resumes from students in your field.
List everything from the last four years: classes, projects, jobs, clubs, volunteering, awards, and skills.
Write each entry as 2–3 bullets that start with an action verb and show a result or a number where you can.
Fit it on one page with your name, school email, phone, and LinkedIn URL at the top.
Get it reviewed at your career center or writing center, then save it as a PDF named Firstname-Lastname-Resume.
goals.doneWhen: You have a one-page PDF resume that someone at your career center or writing center has reviewed.

late.title: Write your resume
steps: Look at two or three sample resumes from students in your field and year.
List your college classes, projects, jobs, clubs, volunteering, awards, and skills.
Write each entry as 2–3 bullets that start with an action verb and show a result or a number where you can.
Fit it on one page with your name, school email, phone, and LinkedIn URL at the top.
Get it reviewed at your career center or writing center, then save it as a PDF named Firstname-Lastname-Resume.
late.doneWhen: You have a one-page PDF resume that someone at your career center or writing center has reviewed.

goals.title: Update and get your resume reviewed
goals.why: A resume goes stale every semester you gain experience.
steps: Add everything new since your last version: jobs, projects, leadership roles, research, and new skills.
Shorten or cut older items, like high school, to keep it to one page.
Rewrite bullets to lead with results: what changed because of your work, with numbers where possible.
Make a version tailored to the roles you'll apply to next, using words from 2–3 real postings.
Have it reviewed at your career center before your next application or career fair.
goals.doneWhen: Your resume is current, one page, tailored to your next applications, and reviewed this year.

goals.title: Research 3 careers on O*NET and BLS
goals.why: Know what the jobs involve and pay before you optimize for them.
steps: Take the free O*NET Interest Profiler to see careers that match your interests.
Pick 3 careers and read each one's O*NET page for daily tasks, skills, and education needed.
Look up each in the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook for pay, job growth, and how people get in.
Write down, for each career, one thing that excites you and one question you still have.
Bring your questions to a career advisor or an informational interview.
goals.doneWhen: You've written a short comparison of 3 careers (tasks, pay, outlook, path in) and know which to explore next.

goals.title: File the FAFSA (every year)
goals.deadline: Before NJ state deadlines in spring; file as early as October
goals.why: Missing it can cost thousands in grants.
steps: Create your StudentAid.gov account, and have a parent create one too if you're a dependent student.
Gather your Social Security number, tax information, and records of savings and income.
File the FAFSA as soon as it opens each fall and list your school; New Jersey state aid has its own deadlines.
Watch your email for your FAFSA Submission Summary and fix anything it flags.
Check your school's financial aid portal for missing documents, then accept your aid offer.
goals.doneWhen: Your FAFSA is submitted for next year, its summary shows no open issues, and your school lists no missing documents.

goals.title: Check EOF, TAG, Garden State Guarantee, and tuition assistance eligibility
goals.why: Money pressure is the most common reason students skip unpaid or low-paid experience.
steps: Read the eligibility rules for the NJ Tuition Aid Grant, the Garden State Guarantee, and EOF on the linked pages.
File the FAFSA, or the NJ Alternative Financial Aid Application if you can't file the FAFSA, since New Jersey uses it for state aid.
If EOF fits you, contact your campus EOF office about how to apply.
Ask your financial aid office whether you qualify for tuition assistance or any grant you aren't getting yet.
Write down each program you qualify for and what keeps it renewed (credits, GPA, deadlines).
goals.doneWhen: You know which state and campus aid programs you qualify for and what you must do each year to keep them.

goals.title: Write and practice a 30-second introduction
goals.why: You'll use it at every fair, info session, and coffee chat.
steps: Write 3–4 sentences: your year and major, what you've done that's relevant, what you're looking for, and a question for the listener.
Make a career-fair version and a shorter one for networking events and info sessions.
Read it out loud and time it; keep it to about 30 seconds and cut anything that sounds memorized.
Practice it with a friend or career advisor and ask what they remember afterward.
Use it at your next career fair, info session, or club event.
goals.doneWhen: You can introduce yourself naturally in about 30 seconds and have used it with someone new.

goals.title: Write a reusable cover letter template
goals.why: Many internship and fellowship applications still ask for one.
steps: Read a cover letter guide and one or two sample letters.
Write a one-page template: an opening that names the role and why you want it, one or two paragraphs linking your experience to the job, and a short close.
Mark the sentences you'll change for each employer (company name, role, what drew you to them).
Get feedback from your writing center or career center.
Save it so a tailored letter takes about 20 minutes per application.
goals.doneWhen: You have a reviewed, one-page cover letter template with clear spots to tailor for each job.

goals.title: Do a mock interview with your career center
goals.why: Interview skill is trainable; most students only practice live.
steps: Learn the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for 'Tell me about a time…' questions.
Write 3–5 short stories from classes, jobs, and clubs that show teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, and a mistake you learned from.
Book a mock interview with your career center through Handshake and send them a job posting to practice for.
Ask for honest feedback on your answers, body language, and the questions you ask at the end.
Rework your two weakest answers and practice them again.
goals.doneWhen: You've done a mock interview, have 3–5 STAR stories ready, and have practiced your weakest answers again.

goals.title: Keep your GPA at or above 3.0
goals.why: Many programs (McNair, co-ops, fellowships, federal internships) screen at 2.5–3.0.
steps: Check your current GPA and what grades this term keep you at 3.0 or above.
Go to office hours in your hardest class by week 3, before the first exam.
Use your campus tutoring or learning center for any class where you're below a B.
Talk to your academic advisor before the withdrawal deadline if a class is going badly.
Plan next term so your hardest classes are spread out rather than stacked.
goals.doneWhen: You finish the term with a GPA of 3.0 or higher.

goals.title: Build a complete LinkedIn profile
goals.why: Recruiters search LinkedIn first; it's also how alumni will check you out after a chat.
steps: Add a clear headshot and a headline that says what you study and what you want, such as 'Packaging Engineering student | Seeking a co-op'.
Write a 3–4 sentence About section: what you study, what you've done, and what you want to do next.
Add your education, jobs, projects, and clubs with 1–2 bullets each, matching your resume.
List at least 5 skills and add relevant courses and projects.
Set a custom profile URL with your name and put it on your resume and email signature.
Turn on job alerts for 2–3 roles you want, and follow 10 companies you'd like to work for.
goals.doneWhen: Your profile has a photo, headline, About section, experience, skills, and a custom URL, and job alerts are on.

goals.title: Connect with 50 relevant people (classmates, alumni, speakers)
goals.why: Warm connections turn into referrals, which beat cold applications.
steps: Start with people you know: classmates, club members, coworkers, and professors.
Use your school's LinkedIn alumni page to find 15–20 alumni in your target field or companies.
Send each a connection request with a short personal note saying how you're connected and why you're reaching out.
Connect with speakers and recruiters you meet at events within 24 hours, mentioning where you met.
Ask 2–3 of your new alumni connections for a 15-minute informational chat.
goals.doneWhen: You have 50+ connections relevant to your field, including alumni and people you've met at events.

goals.title: Post or engage on LinkedIn monthly (projects, events, wins)
goals.why: Visible work keeps you in recruiters' feeds before you apply.
steps: Once a month, post about something you did: a project, an event, a certification, or something you learned.
Keep posts short: what you did, what you learned, and a thank-you to anyone who helped.
Comment thoughtfully on posts from people and companies in your field a few times a month.
Update your profile whenever you add a role, project, or skill.
goals.doneWhen: You've posted or shared something meaningful at least once a month for a semester.

goals.title: Get a professional headshot and email signature
goals.why: Small polish that makes every profile and email look intentional.
steps: Get a headshot: look for free headshot booths at campus career events, or have a friend take one against a plain wall in daylight.
Use the same photo on LinkedIn and Handshake.
Set up a signature in your school email: full name, school, major, graduation year, and LinkedIn URL.
Keep the signature to 3–4 lines with no images or quotes.
goals.doneWhen: You have a professional headshot on LinkedIn and Handshake and an email signature on your school email.

goals.title: Set up GitHub with a profile README
goals.why: Tech hiring managers often check GitHub before the resume.
steps: Create a GitHub account with a professional username and add your photo, name, and school.
Create a profile README with a short intro, what you're learning, and links to your best work.
Pin 3–6 repositories, each with a README that explains what it does and how to run it.
Apply for the GitHub Student Developer Pack with your school email.
Add your GitHub link to your resume and LinkedIn.
goals.doneWhen: Your GitHub has a profile README, pinned projects with READMEs, and is linked from your resume.

goals.title: Commit code consistently for a semester (3+ days a week)
goals.why: A steady contribution graph signals real, ongoing practice.
steps: Pick one project or practice routine to work on all semester, such as a personal project or coding problems.
Schedule 3 or more short sessions a week and commit your work each time.
Write commit messages that say what changed.
Check your contribution graph monthly and adjust your schedule if you're slipping.
goals.doneWhen: Your contribution graph shows activity 3+ days a week for a full semester.

goals.title: Get your first pull request merged into an open-source project
goals.why: Proves you can read someone else's code and work through review.
steps: Practice the fork-and-pull-request workflow on a beginner repository built for first contributions.
Find 2–3 projects you use or like with issues labeled 'good first issue', and read their contributing guidelines.
Comment on an issue to ask whether you can take it, then make the change in a new branch.
Open a pull request that explains what you changed and why, and respond to review comments.
goals.doneWhen: At least one of your pull requests has been merged into a project you don't own.

goals.title: Publish a portfolio site with 3 projects
goals.why: A link that shows your work does more than a bullet that describes it.
steps: Pick your 3 strongest projects and write a short case study for each: the problem, what you did, tools, and the result.
Build a simple site with GitHub Pages or a portfolio platform, with an About page and a contact link.
Add images, demos, or links for each project.
Ask a friend to look at it on a phone and fix anything confusing.
Put the link on your resume, LinkedIn, and GitHub.
goals.doneWhen: Your site is live with 3 project write-ups and linked from your resume.

goals.title: Build a portfolio of 3–5 published writing samples
goals.why: Communication, policy, and PR employers ask for clips or writing samples.
steps: Pitch or submit work to student media, a campus publication, a club newsletter, or a blog in your field.
Aim for pieces that show range, such as news, features, analysis, or opinion.
Save each published piece's link and a PDF copy in case it goes offline.
Collect your best 3–5 on one page, like a portfolio site or Muck Rack profile, with a one-line description of each.
goals.doneWhen: You have 3–5 published pieces collected on one page you can link from your resume.

goals.title: Publish a Kaggle notebook or finish a competition
goals.why: A public analysis is concrete proof of data skills.
steps: Create a Kaggle account and finish one free Kaggle Learn course in Python, pandas, or machine learning.
Pick a beginner competition or a public dataset in a field you care about.
Write a notebook that explores the data, explains each step in plain language, and shows results.
Publish it publicly and link it from your resume or GitHub.
goals.doneWhen: You have a public notebook or a competition submission you can link to.

goals.title: Create an ORCID iD and list your posters and papers
goals.why: Grad programs and journals expect a research identity.
steps: Register for a free ORCID iD.
Add your school, research position, and any posters, presentations, or papers.
Link it from your LinkedIn or personal site and use it whenever you submit work.
goals.doneWhen: You have an ORCID iD listing your research work.

goals.title: Learn core Excel (lookups, pivots, charts)
goals.why: Shows up in most business, health, and policy roles.
steps: Work through a free Excel course covering XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP, PivotTables, and charts.
Practice on a real dataset, such as a club budget or a public dataset.
Build one file that uses a lookup, a PivotTable, and a chart to answer a real question.
Add Excel to your resume with that project as proof.
goals.doneWhen: You can build a lookup, a PivotTable, and a chart from scratch without notes.

goals.title: Build a three-statement financial model
goals.why: Standard technical screen for finance internships.
steps: Learn how the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement connect.
Follow a free modeling course step by step to build a three-statement model.
Build your own model for a real public company from its annual report.
Check that the balance sheet balances, then add best, base, and worst cases.
goals.doneWhen: You've built a working three-statement model for a real company on your own.

goals.title: Learn Python basics
goals.why: The most transferable programming language across fields.
steps: Pick one free course, such as CS50's Python course or freeCodeCamp, and do a little every week.
Learn variables, loops, functions, lists and dictionaries, and reading files.
Write 3 small programs that solve real problems for you, like cleaning data or automating a task.
Put your code on GitHub with a short README for each.
goals.doneWhen: You can write a small Python program from scratch and have 3 on GitHub.

goals.title: Learn SQL
goals.why: Most analyst postings list SQL.
steps: Do an interactive SQL tutorial covering SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, and aggregate functions.
Load a public dataset into a free database tool.
Write 10 queries that answer real questions about the data.
Save the queries and results in a GitHub repository with a short write-up.
goals.doneWhen: You can write queries with joins and group-bys on your own and have examples to show.

goals.title: Build a dashboard in Tableau or Power BI
goals.why: Turning data into a clear picture is what gets analysts noticed.
steps: Get a free student license for Tableau or use Power BI's free desktop app.
Follow a beginner tutorial to connect data and build basic charts.
Choose a public dataset and three questions it can answer.
Build a one-page dashboard that answers them, and publish it or save it for your portfolio.
goals.doneWhen: You have a dashboard that answers clear questions with real data and that you can show.

goals.title: Learn R or SPSS for statistics
goals.why: Research labs and public health jobs run on statistical software.
steps: Check which tool your major uses, R or SPSS, and whether your school provides it.
Take a free beginner course or your department's stats lab sessions.
Reproduce an analysis from a class or paper: descriptive statistics, a t-test or regression, and a chart.
Save your script and output as a short write-up you can show.
goals.doneWhen: You can run and explain a basic analysis in R or SPSS on your own.

goals.title: Solve 100 data structures and algorithms problems
goals.why: Coding interviews for software roles still test this.
steps: Learn the core topics in order: arrays and strings, hash maps, two pointers, stacks and queues, trees, graphs, and dynamic programming.
Solve 3–5 problems a week, starting with easy ones, and track them in a spreadsheet.
For each problem you miss, write down the pattern and redo it a week later.
Do a timed mock interview with a friend once a month, explaining your thinking out loud.
goals.doneWhen: You've solved 100 problems across all core topics and can explain your solutions out loud.

goals.title: Use Git and GitHub for every project
goals.why: Version control is assumed on day one of any tech job.
steps: Complete GitHub's free Introduction to GitHub course.
Keep every class or personal project in Git and commit often with clear messages.
Practice branches and pull requests, even on your own projects.
Learn to fix common problems, like merge conflicts and undoing a commit.
goals.doneWhen: Every project you work on lives in a Git repository with a clean commit history.

goals.title: Get proficient in CAD (SOLIDWORKS or Onshape)
goals.why: Mechanical and device design postings list CAD first.
steps: Get free student access to SOLIDWORKS or Onshape.
Work through the official beginner tutorials: sketches, extrudes, assemblies, and drawings.
Model 3 real objects around you, including one assembly with moving parts.
Make a dimensioned drawing of one of them and add images to your portfolio.
goals.doneWhen: You can model parts and an assembly and produce a dimensioned drawing on your own.

goals.title: Learn MATLAB
goals.why: Common in engineering coursework and R&D roles.
steps: Complete MathWorks' free MATLAB Onramp.
Learn arrays, plotting, scripts, and functions.
Use MATLAB for a class assignment or lab analysis instead of a calculator or spreadsheet.
Save one well-commented script that shows your work.
goals.doneWhen: You've finished MATLAB Onramp and used MATLAB for a real assignment.

goals.title: Learn Figma and design one app flow
goals.why: The standard tool for UX and product design portfolios.
steps: Sign up for Figma's free education plan.
Follow Figma's beginner tutorials on frames, components, and prototyping.
Pick a real app task, like booking a study room, and sketch the steps.
Design and prototype a 4–6 screen flow, test it with 2 people, and revise it.
Add it to your portfolio with a short note on what you changed and why.
goals.doneWhen: You have a clickable prototype of one app flow, tested with real people, in your portfolio.

goals.title: Earn Google Ads/Analytics and HubSpot certifications
goals.why: Free, fast, and listed in entry-level digital marketing postings.
steps: Complete Google's free Skillshop training and pass a Google Ads or Analytics certification.
Complete a free HubSpot Academy certification, such as Inbound or Content Marketing.
Apply what you learned to a real account: a club's social media, a campus event, or a small business.
Add the certifications and results to LinkedIn and your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You hold at least one Google and one HubSpot certification and have used them on a real project.

goals.title: Give 3 presentations outside class (club, Toastmasters, symposium)
goals.why: Presentation skill is one of the top things employers ask for.
steps: Find 3 chances to present outside class: a club meeting, a research symposium, an info session, or a Toastmasters club.
Structure each talk around one main point, three supports, and a clear close.
Rehearse out loud at least twice, ideally recorded or in front of a friend.
Ask for feedback after each talk and pick one thing to improve next time.
goals.doneWhen: You've given 3 presentations outside class and improved something each time.

goals.title: Write a memo or policy brief and get feedback
goals.why: Clear short writing is a daily skill in policy, business, and health jobs.
steps: Read a guide to memo format: heading, purpose, key points first, and a clear request.
Pick a real issue in your field or on campus and write a one-to-two page memo or policy brief.
Get feedback from your writing center or a professor.
Revise it and keep it as a writing sample for applications.
goals.doneWhen: You have a revised memo or brief, reviewed by someone else, ready to use as a writing sample.

goals.title: Reach conversational level in a second language
goals.why: Valued in public service, healthcare, and international business.
steps: Pick the language most useful for your field or community.
Take a course for credit or join a campus conversation group.
Practice a little every day and speak with native speakers at least once a week.
Check your level each semester with a placement test or your instructor.
goals.doneWhen: You can hold a 10-minute conversation on everyday and work topics.

goals.title: Learn core lab techniques in a research lab
goals.why: Lab skills on a resume are what get industry and research offers.
steps: Join a research lab, or take a lab course with hands-on methods.
Complete the lab's required safety training before you start.
Learn the lab's core methods one at a time with a graduate student or postdoc, keeping a detailed notebook.
Ask to run a technique on your own once you've done it under supervision.
goals.doneWhen: You can run the lab's core techniques on your own and record them properly.

goals.title: Complete 20 hands-on security labs or a CTF
goals.why: Security hiring rewards hands-on proof over coursework.
steps: Create free accounts on TryHackMe and picoCTF.
Start with beginner paths on networking, Linux, and web basics.
Complete 20 labs or a CTF, writing short notes on what you learned from each.
Publish a few write-ups on GitHub or a blog for challenges that have ended.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed 20 labs or a CTF and have write-ups you can show.

goals.title: Complete Bloomberg Market Concepts
goals.why: Common talking point and resume line in finance interviews.
steps: Ask your library or business school whether Bloomberg Market Concepts is free through their terminals.
Complete the modules on economics, currencies, fixed income, and equities.
Add the certificate to LinkedIn and your resume.
Practice explaining one recent market event for interviews.
goals.doneWhen: You've finished Bloomberg Market Concepts and can talk about a current market story.

goals.title: Join 1–2 organizations tied to your field
goals.why: The easiest source of peers, mentors, and leadership roles.
steps: Browse your campus student organization directory and the professional societies tied to your major.
Go to one meeting each for 3–4 groups early in the semester.
Join the 1–2 you'd keep showing up to and where you can help with projects or events.
Volunteer for one small task, like an event or a committee, in your first month.
goals.doneWhen: You're a regular member of 1–2 organizations and have helped with at least one event or project.

goals.title: Take an officer or project-lead role
goals.why: Leadership is one of the strongest signals on an early-career resume.
steps: Take on a committee or project role first, so members know your work.
Ask current officers what each role involves and when elections happen.
Run for a position, or volunteer to lead a project or event.
Set one measurable goal for your term, such as members, events, or funds raised, so you have a result to talk about.
goals.doneWhen: You hold an officer or project-lead role and have a concrete result from it.

goals.title: Hold a part-time or campus job
goals.why: Any job builds reliability, and many students need the income.
steps: Search campus jobs in Handshake and your school's student employment site; check work-study listings if you have Federal Work-Study.
Prioritize jobs that build skills for your field, like labs, libraries, IT help desks, tutoring, or offices.
Apply with your resume and a short note on why you want the role.
Keep a running list of what you accomplish on the job to add to your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You hold a part-time or campus job.

goals.title: Volunteer with a community organization
goals.why: Builds perspective and stories for interviews; required for some health paths.
steps: Pick a cause tied to your interests or field, such as health, education, justice, or the environment.
Find opportunities through your campus community engagement office or local nonprofits.
Commit to a regular schedule, like 2–4 hours a week for a semester, rather than one-off events.
Track your hours and what you did so you can describe your impact later.
goals.doneWhen: You volunteer regularly with one organization and have logged your hours.

goals.title: Work as a research assistant with a professor
goals.why: Opens recommendation letters and research summers.
steps: Browse your department's faculty pages and your campus research office's listings, and pick 5–8 labs whose work interests you.
Read one recent paper or project summary from each lab.
Email each professor a short note: who you are, what interests you about their work, your availability, and your resume.
Follow up once after 1–2 weeks, and ask about volunteer, course-credit, or paid options.
Once you join, show up reliably and ask your mentor what success looks like after one semester.
goals.doneWhen: You have a research position with a professor or lab.

goals.title: Do a paid summer research program
goals.why: The core experience for PhD and research-industry paths.
steps: List 5–10 programs that fit your field and note their deadlines, which are usually December to February.
Ask 2 professors for recommendation letters at least 4 weeks before the first deadline.
Write a statement about your research interests and what you hope to learn.
Submit every application on time and track them in a spreadsheet.
goals.doneWhen: You've accepted a paid summer research position.

goals.title: Complete an honors thesis or independent research project
goals.why: Top signal for grad school and research careers.
steps: Ask your department about honors thesis requirements and deadlines during junior year.
Find a faculty advisor, usually someone whose lab or class you already know.
Write a one-page proposal with your question, methods, and timeline.
Apply for campus research funding if your project needs it.
Meet your advisor regularly and present your results at a campus symposium.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed and submitted or defended your thesis or independent project.

goals.title: Build and ship a personal project
goals.why: Something you built is the best answer to 'tell me about a project.'
steps: Pick a problem you or your friends actually have, and keep the first version small.
Write down what 'done' means for version 1 in 3–5 features.
Build it in small steps, committing to GitHub as you go.
Ship it: publish, deploy, or share it with real users, and collect feedback.
Write a README with screenshots and add the project to your resume.
goals.doneWhen: Your project is live or usable by others and documented on GitHub.

goals.title: Compete in a hackathon
goals.why: Fast team experience and recruiter exposure in a weekend.
steps: Find a hackathon on your campus or on MLH's event list and register early, since spots fill up.
Team up with 2–3 people, or join team-forming at the start.
Go to the beginner workshops, pick an idea you can demo in the time limit, and build the smallest working version.
Practice a 2-minute demo and submit your project with a short write-up.
goals.doneWhen: You've competed in a hackathon and submitted a working project.

goals.title: Join an engineering design team (Formula SAE, robotics, etc.)
goals.why: Hands-on build experience that engineering recruiters ask about first.
steps: Find your school's engineering design teams (Formula SAE, robotics, and others) at the involvement fair or engineering school site.
Attend recruitment meetings early in the fall.
Join a subteam that matches your interests and commit to its weekly build sessions.
Take ownership of one part or system so you have a concrete contribution to describe.
goals.doneWhen: You're an active team member responsible for a specific part or system.

goals.title: Compete in a case competition
goals.why: Shows business problem-solving under pressure; firms recruit at them.
steps: Find competitions through your business school, consulting or finance clubs, and professional groups.
Form a team of 3–4 with mixed strengths: analysis, slides, and presenting.
Practice on old cases: define the problem, structure the analysis, and back your recommendation with numbers.
Rehearse your presentation and practice answering tough questions.
goals.doneWhen: You've competed in a case competition and presented your recommendation.

goals.title: Complete 2 virtual job simulations
goals.why: A quick way to test a field and get interview stories before your first internship.
steps: Browse free virtual job simulations on Forage for companies or roles in your field.
Complete two simulations, taking notes on the tasks you did.
Add them to your resume and LinkedIn as projects, naming the skills you used.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed two simulations and added them to your resume.

goals.title: Do a first internship or career-related summer job
goals.why: Any relevant summer experience makes the junior-year internship far easier to land.
steps: Read a first- and second-year internship search guide so you know where to look.
Search Handshake for first-year-friendly roles, summer programs, and campus jobs related to your field.
Ask your career center and professors about early programs, many of which are built for students without experience.
Apply to 10–15 options with a tailored resume.
goals.doneWhen: You've accepted a summer internship or career-related job.

goals.title: Do an internship in your target field
goals.why: Junior-summer internships are the main pipeline to full-time offers.
steps: Make a list of 20–30 employers in your target field.
Set up Handshake and LinkedIn job alerts for those employers and roles.
Reach out to alumni at your top employers for advice and, if it goes well, a referral.
Apply as postings open (many open in late summer and fall for the next summer) and prepare STAR stories for interviews.
goals.doneWhen: You've accepted an internship in your target field.

goals.title: Complete a 6-month co-op
goals.why: Deeper than an internship and often converts to a job offer.
steps: Meet your school's co-op office to learn how co-op terms, credit, and timing work for your major.
Plan which semesters you'll be away so your required courses still fit.
Apply through the co-op office and Handshake, tailoring your resume to each employer.
Prepare for interviews with the STAR method.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed a co-op placement.

goals.title: Shadow professionals for 40+ hours
goals.why: Health programs want proof you know what the job is.
steps: Ask physicians or professionals you already know first, then your pre-health office, professors, and local hospitals.
Email a short, polite request with your goals and availability.
Shadow in more than one setting or specialty if you can.
Keep a log of dates, hours, and what you learned after each session.
Send a thank-you note after each shadowing experience.
goals.doneWhen: You've logged 40+ hours of shadowing with notes from each session.

goals.title: Log 150+ hours of patient-care experience
goals.why: Medical, PA, and PT schools screen on hands-on patient care.
steps: Choose a role with direct patient contact: EMT, CNA, medical scribe, patient-care technician, or hospital volunteer.
Complete any training or certification the role needs.
Commit to a regular schedule, such as one shift a week.
Log your hours and a few patient interactions that taught you something.
goals.doneWhen: You've logged 150+ patient-care hours with notes on what you learned.

goals.title: Complete a nursing externship
goals.why: Hospitals often hire new grads from their own extern pools.
steps: Ask your nursing school about externship timing and hospital partners; most are the summer before senior year.
Research hospital externship programs and their deadlines, which often fall in winter.
Get your resume and references ready and keep your BLS current.
Apply to several programs and prepare for interviews.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed a nursing externship.

goals.title: Work as a licensed pharmacy intern
goals.why: Paid experience that also builds residency and job references.
steps: Register as a pharmacist intern with the New Jersey Board of Pharmacy once your program says you're eligible.
Apply for intern roles at community, hospital, or specialty pharmacies.
Track your intern hours the way your program requires.
goals.doneWhen: You're registered and working as a pharmacy intern.

goals.title: Complete your BSW field placement
goals.why: Required for the degree and for advanced-standing MSW programs.
steps: Attend your BSW program's field orientation and complete its placement application on time.
List the populations and settings you want to work with.
Interview with the agencies your field office suggests.
Complete the required hours and supervision, and keep your field log current.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed your BSW field placement hours.

goals.title: Produce work for student media (newspaper, radio, or TV)
goals.why: Published work is the entry ticket for media and PR roles.
steps: Find your campus newspaper, radio, or TV station and go to an open meeting or training.
Start with small assignments and meet every deadline.
Ask editors for feedback and take on a regular beat or show.
Save links to your published work for your portfolio.
goals.doneWhen: You've published or produced several pieces for student media.

goals.title: Intern in a government or campaign office
goals.why: Public-sector jobs hire from people they already know.
steps: List offices that match your interests: your state legislator, a member of Congress, a city or county office, or a campaign.
Check deadlines early, since many legislative and congressional internships open months before each term.
Apply with your resume, a writing sample, and a short cover letter.
Ask your school about credit and funding for unpaid placements.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed an internship in a government or campaign office.

goals.title: Observe court, do a ride-along, or volunteer in reentry
goals.why: Shows you understand the system you want to work in.
steps: Ask your criminal justice department or advisor about court observation, ride-alongs, and reentry programs.
Sit in on a public court session and take notes on the roles and procedures.
Ask a local police department whether it offers ride-alongs through a community program.
Volunteer with a reentry or legal aid organization and reflect on what you learned.
goals.doneWhen: You've done at least two of: court observation, a ride-along, and reentry volunteering.

goals.title: Study or intern abroad
goals.why: Builds independence and global perspective; Gilman covers costs for Pell recipients.
steps: Meet your study abroad office by your second year to see programs that fit your major.
Plan with your academic advisor which courses will transfer back.
Apply for funding, such as the Gilman Scholarship if you receive a Pell Grant, plus campus awards.
Submit your program application and passport paperwork on time.
goals.doneWhen: You've studied or interned abroad.

goals.title: Pitch a venture or join a startup
goals.why: Teaches selling an idea and moving fast.
steps: Join your campus entrepreneurship club or attend a startup event.
Write a one-page summary of your idea: the problem, who has it, and your solution.
Talk to 10 potential customers about the problem before building anything.
Pitch at a campus competition, or join an early-stage startup as an intern.
goals.doneWhen: You've pitched a venture or worked at a startup.

goals.title: Tutor or work as a teaching assistant
goals.why: Teaching proves mastery and builds faculty relationships.
steps: Ask the professor of a course you did well in about TA or grader openings.
Apply to your campus learning or tutoring center.
Complete any tutor training they offer.
Ask students for feedback and keep track of what works.
goals.doneWhen: You're working as a tutor or teaching assistant.

goals.title: Attend your first career fair (to look, not to land)
goals.why: Low-pressure practice before the fairs that count.
steps: Check your campus career fair's employer list in Handshake and pick 5 employers to visit.
Read each employer's website so you can ask one real question.
Bring copies of your resume and practice your 30-second introduction.
Talk to your 5 employers, ask about opportunities for students in your year, and collect names.
Send each person a short thank-you message or LinkedIn request within a day.
goals.doneWhen: You've talked with 5 employers at a career fair and followed up with each.

goals.title: Work a career fair with a target list of employers
goals.why: Fall junior-year fairs feed most junior-summer internships.
steps: Two weeks before, rank 8–10 employers with open roles that fit you.
Apply online to their postings before the fair when possible.
Prepare a tailored pitch and two specific questions for each top employer.
At the fair, visit your top choices first, ask about next steps, and get contact information.
Follow up within 24 hours, referring to your conversation.
goals.doneWhen: You've met your target employers, applied to their roles, and followed up with each.

goals.title: Do 5 informational interviews with alumni
goals.why: The fastest way to learn what a job is really like and get referred.
steps: Find alumni in roles you're curious about using your school's LinkedIn alumni page.
Send a short message asking for 15–20 minutes to learn about their path, not for a job.
Prepare 5–8 questions about their work, how they got there, and advice for someone in your position.
Keep the call on time, ask who else they'd suggest you talk to, and send a thank-you within 24 hours.
Keep a simple log of whom you talked to and what you learned.
goals.doneWhen: You've had 5 informational interviews and sent a thank-you after each.

goals.title: Build relationships with 2 professors (office hours, research)
goals.why: You'll need recommendation letters for research, fellowships, and grad school.
steps: Go to office hours in the first few weeks of each semester, even just to introduce yourself.
Read your professors' faculty pages and ask about their research or career path.
Return regularly with questions about the material or your goals.
Stay in touch after the class ends with a short email or a visit once a semester.
goals.doneWhen: Two professors know you by name, know your goals, and could write you a letter.

goals.title: Find a mentor in your target field
goals.why: A mentor shortens every decision on this map.
steps: Decide what you want help with: choosing a path, landing internships, or a specific field.
Look for potential mentors among professors, alumni, supervisors, and program advisors such as SEO, MLT, or INROADS.
Start with a small ask, like a 20-minute conversation, rather than asking someone to be your mentor.
If it goes well, suggest a regular check-in (monthly works for most people) and bring questions each time.
goals.doneWhen: You meet regularly with someone in your target field who gives you advice.

goals.title: Join a professional society as a student member
goals.why: Student rates are cheap and give access to scholarships, job boards, and conferences.
steps: Find the main professional society for your field and its student membership rate, which is often discounted.
Join, and check whether your campus has a student chapter.
Use member benefits: job boards, scholarships, mentoring, and webinars.
Attend at least one chapter or society event each semester.
goals.doneWhen: You're a student member and have attended at least one event.

goals.title: Attend a national conference or diversity career conference
goals.why: Conference career fairs often interview on the spot.
steps: Choose a national or diversity career conference in your field and check student registration and travel scholarships.
Ask your department, student organization, or school about funding.
Before you go, list the companies and sessions you want and prepare your resume and pitch.
Collect contacts and follow up within a week.
goals.doneWhen: You've attended a conference and followed up with the people you met.

goals.title: Attend 3 employer info sessions
goals.why: Recruiters remember the people who showed up.
steps: Check Handshake events for employer info sessions and workshops in your field.
RSVP to 3 sessions this semester.
Prepare one question for each, and introduce yourself to a presenter afterward.
Follow up on LinkedIn with anyone you spoke to.
goals.doneWhen: You've attended 3 info sessions and connected with at least one presenter.

goals.title: Get CPR/BLS certified
goals.why: Required for nearly every clinical job and volunteer role.
steps: Find an American Heart Association or Red Cross BLS class; many campuses and hospitals offer them.
Complete the course and its skills test.
Save your card and its expiration date, usually two years out, and add it to your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You hold a current BLS card.

goals.title: Earn EMT certification
goals.why: Fastest route to paid patient-care hours.
steps: Find a state-approved EMT course; some campus EMS squads sponsor training.
Complete the course and its clinical hours.
Pass the certification exam your course prepares you for and apply for New Jersey certification.
Join a campus or local squad to start logging patient-care hours.
goals.doneWhen: You're a certified EMT.

goals.title: Earn the RBT credential
goals.why: Common paid clinical job for psychology students.
steps: Complete the 40-hour RBT training; many programs are online.
Complete the competency assessment with a qualified supervisor.
Apply to the BACB, pass the background check, and pass the RBT exam.
Work in a supervised role at an ABA provider to keep the credential active.
goals.doneWhen: You hold the RBT credential.

goals.title: Become a certified pharmacy technician
goals.why: Paid pharmacy experience while in school.
steps: Complete a pharmacy technician training program or the required work experience.
Register for the PTCB's CPhT exam.
Study with the official content outline and practice exams.
Pass the exam and register as a pharmacy technician with the New Jersey Board of Pharmacy.
goals.doneWhen: You're a certified pharmacy technician.

goals.title: Earn the aPHR
goals.why: Entry-level HR certification with no experience requirement.
steps: Read HRCI's aPHR eligibility and exam outline; no HR experience is required.
Study with a prep course for 6–10 weeks.
Schedule and pass the exam.
Add it to your resume and LinkedIn.
goals.doneWhen: You've earned the aPHR.

goals.title: Sit for the CHES exam
goals.why: Recognized credential for health education roles.
steps: Check that your coursework meets NCHEC's eligibility requirements.
Register for the CHES exam window that follows your graduation.
Study with the official exam outline and practice questions.
Sit for the exam.
goals.doneWhen: You've sat for the CHES exam.

goals.title: Earn ACSM or NSCA certification
goals.why: Required for many fitness and strength roles.
steps: Choose ACSM or NSCA based on the jobs you want: clinical, personal training, or strength and conditioning.
Check eligibility; some certifications require a degree and current CPR/AED.
Study with the certifying body's official materials.
Schedule and pass the exam.
goals.doneWhen: You hold an ACSM or NSCA certification.

goals.title: Earn CompTIA Security+ or ISC2 CC
goals.why: Baseline credential for security and many government IT jobs.
steps: Choose ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (entry level) or CompTIA Security+.
Study the official exam objectives and do hands-on labs alongside.
Take practice exams until you score comfortably above passing.
Schedule and pass the exam, then add it to your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You hold Security+ or ISC2 CC.

goals.title: Earn an entry cloud certification (AWS Cloud Practitioner)
goals.why: Cloud shows up in most modern software and IT roles.
steps: Sign up for AWS's free Cloud Practitioner training through AWS Educate or AWS Skill Builder.
Learn the core services (compute, storage, databases), pricing, and security basics.
Practice in the free tier by deploying a small project.
Take practice questions, then schedule and pass the exam.
goals.doneWhen: You hold the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner or a similar entry cloud certification.

goals.title: Complete a Google Career Certificate
goals.why: Structured, recognized skill credential in data, IT, UX, or project management.
steps: Pick the Google Career Certificate that fits your goals, such as Data Analytics, IT Support, UX Design, or Project Management.
Check whether your school or library offers free access.
Complete the courses and graded projects at a steady weekly pace.
Add the certificate and its portfolio project to LinkedIn and your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed a Google Career Certificate.

goals.title: Earn the SOLIDWORKS CSWA
goals.why: Proves CAD skill on paper.
steps: Get SOLIDWORKS student access.
Review the CSWA exam topics and sample exam.
Practice modeling parts and assemblies under time pressure.
Take and pass the CSWA exam.
goals.doneWhen: You hold the CSWA.

goals.title: Take the FE exam
goals.why: First step to a PE license; easiest while coursework is fresh.
steps: Create an NCEES account and read the FE exam specifications for your discipline.
Schedule the exam for your final year or soon after graduation, while the material is fresh.
Study with the official NCEES practice exam and the FE reference handbook.
Take the exam, then apply for Engineer in Training status once you pass.
goals.doneWhen: You've taken the FE exam.

goals.title: Earn a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt
goals.why: Valued in manufacturing and operations roles.
steps: Choose a reputable Green Belt program; some schools and employers sponsor them.
Learn DMAIC, process mapping, and basic statistics.
Complete a real improvement project if your program requires one.
Pass the exam and add the certification to your resume.
goals.doneWhen: You hold a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt.

goals.title: Earn Microsoft Office Specialist: Excel
goals.why: Turns 'proficient in Excel' into something verifiable.
steps: Ask whether your school offers free Microsoft Office Specialist exams.
Review the official Excel exam objectives.
Practice with official practice tests until you're comfortable with every objective.
Schedule and pass the exam.
goals.doneWhen: You hold Microsoft Office Specialist: Excel.

goals.title: Complete CITI human-subjects training
goals.why: Required before joining most human-subjects labs.
steps: Ask your lab or IRB which CITI courses you need, usually human subjects research.
Log in to CITI through your school.
Complete the modules and quizzes.
Save the completion certificate and send it to your lab.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed the required CITI training and shared the certificate.

goals.title: Plan your path to 150 credit hours for the CPA
goals.why: NJ requires 150 credits; deciding early saves a year or a lot of money.
steps: Read New Jersey's current CPA education requirements; check whether the 150-hour rule or a newer alternative applies to you.
Count the credits you'll have at graduation and how many more you need.
Compare options with your advisor: a master's in accounting, a minor, summer courses, or extra credits during your degree.
Write the plan down by semester with costs, and confirm it covers the required accounting and business courses.
goals.doneWhen: You have a written, semester-by-semester plan to meet New Jersey's CPA education requirement.

late.why: It decides whether you need a master’s or extra credits after graduation, and how to pay for them.

goals.title: Add a minor or certificate that fills a gap (data, writing, a language)
goals.why: A targeted minor can cover what your major doesn't.
steps: Name the gap you want to fill for your target career, such as data skills, writing, or a language.
Look up the minors and certificates at your school that cover it and how many credits each takes.
Check with your advisor how it fits your remaining semesters without delaying graduation.
Declare it and put its courses into your semester plan.
goals.doneWhen: The minor or certificate is declared and its courses are in your semester plan.

goals.title: Apply to the Eagleton Undergraduate Associates program
goals.why: Selective politics program with a stipend and placement network.
steps: Read the Eagleton Undergraduate Associates requirements and timeline; applications open in early fall.
Talk to a past associate or Eagleton staff about what the program looks for.
Ask a professor for a recommendation at least 3 weeks before the deadline.
Draft your essays, get them reviewed at your writing center, and submit on time.
goals.doneWhen: Your application is submitted before the deadline.

goals.title: Meet your campus fellowships office
goals.why: Many awards need a campus nomination a year ahead.
steps: Browse your fellowships office's list of national awards and note 2–3 that fit your goals.
Book an appointment and bring your resume and a few sentences on what you want to do.
Ask about the campus deadlines, which come weeks before the national ones.
Leave with a timeline for any award you'll apply to.
goals.doneWhen: You've met your fellowships office and have a timeline for at least one award.

goals.title: Apply for a national fellowship (Goldwater, Truman, Fulbright, Gilman)
goals.why: Even unsuccessful applications sharpen your story for everything else.
steps: Meet your fellowships office at least 6 months before the national deadline.
Read past winners' profiles and the selection criteria carefully.
Ask recommenders early and give them your materials.
Write and revise your essays with your fellowships advisor to meet the campus deadline.
Submit, and practice for interviews if you advance.
goals.doneWhen: You've submitted a national fellowship application.

goals.title: Prep for your entrance exam (MCAT, LSAT, GRE, PCAT)
goals.why: Gate for professional and graduate school.
steps: Check test dates and score deadlines for your programs and pick a date that leaves time for a retake.
Take a free official practice test to get your baseline score.
Make a study plan (often 2–4 months at 10–15 hours a week) built around your weakest sections.
Use the test maker's official materials first, and take a full practice test every 2–3 weeks.
If cost is a barrier, apply for the test's fee assistance program before you register.
goals.doneWhen: You've taken the exam, or you're registered with practice scores in your target programs' range.

goals.title: Line up 3 recommendation letters
goals.why: Letter writers need months of notice and real knowledge of your work.
steps: Pick 3 people who know your work well: ideally two professors and one supervisor or research mentor.
Ask each at least 4–6 weeks before your first deadline whether they can write a strong letter.
Send them your resume, a draft of your statement, the deadlines, and a short list of what you'd like them to mention.
Send a polite reminder a week before the deadline and a thank-you note once it's submitted.
goals.doneWhen: Three recommenders have agreed and have everything they need, with deadlines confirmed.

goals.title: Build a balanced list of grad or professional programs
goals.why: A balanced list beats applying only to reach schools.
steps: Write down what matters most: field, location, cost and funding, program length, and outcomes.
Research 10–15 programs using their websites and admitted-student data (GPA and test ranges).
Sort them into reach, target, and likely programs based on how your record compares.
Narrow to a balanced list you can afford to apply to, often 6–10, and talk it through with an advisor.
goals.doneWhen: You have a balanced, budgeted list of programs with their deadlines.

goals.title: Draft and revise your personal statement
goals.why: Takes several drafts; start before senior fall.
steps: Read each program's prompt and note what it asks for (your story, your goals, your fit).
Brainstorm 3–4 experiences that show why you want this path, then choose one theme that ties them together.
Write a full rough draft without worrying about length.
Get feedback from your writing center and a pre-professional or faculty advisor, and revise at least twice.
Tailor the final version to each program and proofread it aloud.
goals.doneWhen: You have a final statement, reviewed by at least two people, tailored to each program.

late.why: It takes several drafts, so give yourself a few weeks before your first deadline.

goals.title: Prepare for the NCLEX-RN
goals.why: Licensure gate after graduation.
steps: Read the official NCLEX candidate information so you know the format and how registration works.
Start practice questions in your final year at a steady weekly pace.
Track your weak areas and review them with your nursing program's prep resources.
As graduation nears, apply to the New Jersey Board of Nursing and register for the exam with Pearson VUE.
goals.doneWhen: You've applied to the board, registered for the NCLEX, and your practice results show you're ready.

goals.title: Decide on residency vs. industry vs. community practice
goals.why: Each route has different deadlines and experiences to build.
steps: List the paths you're weighing: residency, industry, and community or hospital practice.
Talk to at least one pharmacist in each path about their day and how they got there.
If residency appeals, read the ASHP residency process and note its timeline for your final year.
Decide by the fall of your next-to-last year so you can plan rotations and applications.
goals.doneWhen: You've chosen a path and planned your rotations and applications around it.

goals.title: Apply to 5 outside scholarships
goals.why: Free money; many awards get few applicants.
steps: Search free sources: your school's scholarship site, professional societies, community groups, and the scholarships linked here.
Make a spreadsheet of 10 options with deadlines, requirements, and essay prompts.
Write one strong base essay you can adapt for each.
Apply to at least 5, starting with the ones that fit you best.
Never pay to apply; skip any 'scholarship' that asks for a fee.
goals.doneWhen: You've submitted 5 outside scholarship applications.

goals.title: Apply to first- and second-year programs (SEO, MLT, INROADS, early-ID)
goals.why: These programs feed directly into the competitive junior internships.
steps: Research early-career programs for first- and second-year students in your field, such as SEO, MLT, INROADS, and company programs.
Note their deadlines, which are often in the fall for the following summer.
Prepare your resume and short answers about your goals.
Apply to 3–5 programs and track their status.
goals.doneWhen: You've applied to at least 3 early-career programs.

goals.title: Apply to summer research programs (REUs, RISE, SURE)
goals.why: Deadlines come months before summer.
steps: Search NSF REU listings and the other programs here for your field, and note deadlines (usually December to February).
Ask 2 professors for letters at least 4 weeks ahead.
Write a research statement: what interests you, what you've done, and what you hope to learn.
Apply to 5–10 programs to improve your odds.
goals.doneWhen: You've applied to at least 5 summer research programs.

goals.title: Apply to 15+ summer opportunities for after sophomore year
goals.deadline: Most summer roles fill by March
goals.why: Sophomore summer experience is what makes junior internships winnable.
steps: Read a first- and second-year internship search guide.
Set up Handshake and LinkedIn job alerts for internships in your field that are open to sophomores.
Tailor your resume to each type of role you're targeting.
Apply to 15 or more, tracking where and when you applied in a spreadsheet.
Follow up with any contacts you have at those companies.
goals.doneWhen: You've applied to 15+ summer opportunities and tracked them.

goals.title: Apply to 30+ target internships for junior summer
goals.deadline: Many large employers recruit August–October of junior year
goals.why: The main recruiting window for full-time offers.
steps: Start in late summer before junior year, when many large employers open applications.
Build a list of 30+ target roles and set job alerts for each company.
Ask alumni at your top companies for a conversation and, if it goes well, a referral.
Apply with a tailored resume (and cover letter when asked) and prepare STAR stories for interviews.
Track every application and follow up after interviews.
goals.doneWhen: You've submitted 30+ applications to target internships.

goals.title: Apply to federal internships on USAJOBS
goals.why: Federal hiring uses its own resume rules and timelines.
steps: Create a USAJOBS profile and save searches for internships and Pathways roles.
Build a federal-style resume with dates, hours per week, and detailed duties; it's longer than a private-sector resume.
Read each announcement's qualifications and use matching wording in your resume.
Apply well before announcements close; some close early once they get enough applicants.
goals.doneWhen: You've applied to federal internships on USAJOBS.

goals.title: Run your full-time job search (or convert a return offer)
goals.why: Many offers go out in senior fall, and hiring continues through spring and summer.
steps: Start in the fall of senior year (earlier in finance and consulting), and if you interned, ask about a return offer.
Pick 2–3 role types and make a list of target employers.
Set job alerts, reach out to alumni, and apply steadily every week.
Practice interviews with your career center and prepare STAR stories.
Track every application and follow up.
goals.doneWhen: You've accepted a full-time offer.

goals.title: Submit graduate or professional school applications
goals.why: Most deadlines fall between September and January of senior year.
steps: Make a calendar of every program's deadlines and requirements.
Order transcripts and send test scores early.
Confirm your recommenders have everything they need.
Tailor your statement to each program and proofread everything.
Ask about application fee waivers before paying.
goals.doneWhen: All your graduate or professional school applications are submitted.

goals.title: Compare and negotiate your offer
goals.why: Many entry-level offers have room to negotiate; few graduates ask.
steps: Get every offer in writing and ask when they need your answer.
Research pay for the role and city using salary sites and your career center's data.
Compare the whole package: salary, bonus, benefits, location, growth, and start date.
Practice with a career advisor, then ask politely for what you want, with evidence.
Get the final terms in writing before you accept, then withdraw from your other processes.
goals.doneWhen: You've compared your offers and accepted one on the best terms you could reach.

goals.title: Enter a student packaging design competition
goals.why: A finished package design is the portfolio piece packaging recruiters ask about.
steps: Look up current student packaging competitions (IoPP AmeriStar Student, PPA, and FPA) and their deadlines.
Form a team or work solo, and pick a real product with a packaging problem.
Design, prototype, and test your package against the competition's criteria.
Submit your entry with clear photos and a write-up, and add it to your portfolio.
goals.doneWhen: You've submitted an entry to a student packaging competition.

goals.title: Add the Rutgers packaging certificate
goals.why: Four packaging courses open packaging and consumer-products roles to engineers in other majors.
steps: Take Introduction to Packaging Engineering (14:440:301), the required first course.
Plan three more packaging courses into your remaining semesters with your advisor.
Confirm with the packaging program how to declare the certificate.
goals.doneWhen: You've completed or scheduled all four packaging courses and declared the certificate.
